residual_risks: SEC-1 is open, not fixed. The human approval at journal seq 319 says "Risk accepted to let the run complete, not resolved" and "nothing from this run is to be deployed anywhere reachable until it is closed". Approving this node does not change that: two customer accounts with plaintexts published in artifacts/openapi.yaml:99-102 are created by V2 on any deploy, there is no registration endpoint so they are the accounts, and SEC-5 makes either one sufficient to permanently take down any link on the service.

AC21 has a working bypass in the shipped code. A trailing dot (https://malware.example.com./x) defeats the denylist (SEC-2), and SEC-6 defeats the internal-address rule with non-dotted-quad literals (http://2130706433/). Both were confirmed by reading plus a standalone JDK 21 probe, not by a test - and no test in the suite would catch either.

An unvalidated {code} path variable reaches Redis, PostgreSQL and abuse_reports.code VARCHAR(64) on the two untrusted paths, and ApiExceptionHandler has no fallback handler behind it (SEC-7/API-1/PERF-6 plus API-2). An over-long code on the abuse endpoint yields a 500 with Spring's default body against a spec that declares the error catalogue closed.

AC3's "exact for the life of the link" rests on an unexercised durable write path (TEST-1: delete @Scheduled from ClickFlushJob and the suite stays green), an unread Lua script (token_bucket.lua read line-by-line by nobody; read_click_deltas.lua audited for cost and injection but not atomicity), a drain ceiling of ~100 distinct links/sec/instance nobody measured (PERF-1), and a Redis eviction policy outside this repository that nobody examined.

Rate limiting is weaker than the contract implies in two ways no test can reveal: the three IP-keyed buckets key on the TCP peer with no forwarded-headers strategy, so behind any load balancer they neither isolate sources nor scale (SEC-3); and the limiter fails open for every bucket including SIGN_IN, so a Redis outage removes brute-force protection while nothing caps concurrent Argon2id at m=16384 KiB across Tomcat's 200 default threads (SEC-4/PERF-8).

Behaviour under a slow-but-alive Redis is assumed rather than measured. A degraded Redis can hold a Hikari connection for up to 100 seconds on one unmetered list request (PERF-3 with SEC-11) against an unsized default pool of 10 (PERF-5), and adds up to ~3s to a redirect across three sequential round trips (PERF-9). No load has been generated against this build at all.

The service's contract with its edge proxy does not exist in written form. Whether /actuator/metrics and /actuator/prometheus (unauthenticated, on the service port, absent from openapi.yaml) reach the internet is decided by configuration in neither the repository nor docs/; TLS, HSTS and HTTP parser differentials between Tomcat and the edge were examined by nobody.

No dependency vulnerability scan has been run by anyone in this pipeline. jjwt 0.12.6, bcprov-jdk18on 1.81, Spring Boot 3.5.16 and their transitives are unchecked against advisories, and no SCA gate exists to catch it on a later run either.

Two acceptance criteria are shipping without a definition, not merely without a test. AC22's "fast" has no published latency number to assert against, and design.json records the threat-check fail-open reading as a blocking ambiguity a human never answered, with TEST-6 confirming neither branch is exercised. Both need a decision from a person.

The abuse takedown accepted in clarification Q4 rests on assumptions that do not hold as built: "rate-limited per reporter" is 60/min (86,400 links/day from one account), the takedown is irreversible with no unblock path and no moderation console, its audit trail is a log an attacker can forge via SEC-9, and an owner's DELETE silently relabels a BLOCKED link as DELETED (API-6). Reversing this reverses a decision a human already signed off.

If this is deployed anyway, missing APP_SESSION_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM/APP_SESSION_PUBLIC_KEY_PEM produces an ephemeral per-instance keypair with only a WARN - every token breaks on restart or scale-out - and a missing APP_BASE_URL silently makes the self-target check protect localhost (SEC-12).

Test-suite health is more fragile than 148/148 suggests: TEST-7 documents cross-class coupling through a JVM-wide Redis where several 404 assertions depend on token-bucket state and wall-clock refill. That is the shape of a test that fails once a month and gets muted, so today's green is weaker evidence than a green with isolated fixtures would be.

Coverage is a line-count (86.9%), not a behaviour measure. The specific paths the review calls unverified - durable click flush, threat-check fail-open/fail-closed, per-source rate-limit isolation, redirect latency - can all be partly line-covered while remaining unasserted.
